why: Dry air is about 78% nitrogen, 21% oxygen, and 1% other gases.
This reverses the major gases: nitrogen, not oxygen, is about 78% of dry air.

Oxygen is about 21%, while nitrogen is about 78%; these proportions are reversed.
Temperature usually increases above the tropopause in the stratosphere; it does not start decreasing there.
The tropopause is the transition boundary between the troposphere and stratosphere.
The mesosphere begins above the stratosphere, not at the tropopause.
This describes the stratosphere above the boundary, not the tropopause itself.
Gpdam measures geopotential height, not temperature.
Fahrenheit is not the standard aviation temperature unit used in Europe and Africa.
Kelvin is a scientific absolute scale, not the unit in routine aviation weather reports.

Condensation releases latent heat into the surrounding air as cloud forms.
Stabilising air does not itself release latent heat; condensation does.
Descending air warms by compression rather than releasing latent heat through condensation.
Evaporation absorbs latent heat, so it cools rather than releases heat.
Condensation releases latent heat, so saturated rising air cools more slowly than unsaturated air.

1°C/100 m is the dry adiabatic rate; saturation lowers the cooling rate.
2°C/1000 ft is the ISA environmental lapse rate, not the dry parcel rate.

0.65°C/100 m is the ISA environmental rate.

250 hPa occurs much higher than FL180 in the ISA.
850 hPa is a much lower altitude pressure level than FL180.

300 hPa is lower than the ISA pressure at FL180.
250 hPa is characteristic of a much higher level.

This is 100 times too small; mass equals density times volume.

This is ten times too large; multiply 1.225 kg/m³ by 1 m³.

5,500 ft is far below the ISA tropopause.
11,000 ft is not 11,000 metres; the standard height is about 36,000 ft.
48,000 ft is substantially higher than the ISA tropopause.

18,000 ft is about half the ISA tropopause height.

why: Above the friction layer, geostrophic wind flows parallel to straight isobars.

Wind does not flow perpendicular to isobars in geostrophic balance.
Isohypses are height contours on pressure-level charts; this asks about a pressure gradient.
Smooth ocean generally produces less friction than rough mountainous terrain.
Rough mountains and vegetation create the greatest drag and reduce wind speed most.
Vegetation adds drag, but flat terrain is less obstructive than mountainous, vegetated terrain.
Flat barren land is relatively smooth and creates less drag than mountainous terrain.
Surface convergence forces air upward, rather than causing descent.
Converging surface air must rise; if moist, it can form cloud.
Descent and cloud dissipation are more consistent with divergence, not convergence.
Ascent is right, but moist rising air favours cloud formation, not dissipation.
Subsidence means sinking air, not horizontal air flowing apart.
Air flowing apart is divergence.
Convergence is air flowing together, the opposite motion.
“Concordence” is not the meteorological term for horizontal outflow.
Divergence means air spreading apart, the opposite of flow together.
Air flowing together is convergence.
“Soncordence” is not the meteorological term; use convergence.
Subsidence is downward motion, not horizontal inflow.

Divergence means flow apart, whereas head-on air masses converge.

Divergence does not describe meeting air masses; convergence causes ascent.

The geographic poles are not the mid-latitude polar front.

Extensive lifting favours lower pressure, not high-pressure centres.

Daytime upslope flow is anabatic wind.

Lee-side solar heating does not directly strengthen windward slope thermals.

Warming aloft is not the local surface-heating mechanism.
Night-time radiative cooling produces downslope katabatic flow, not stronger upslope flow.
Atmospheric water occurs as vapour, liquid droplets, and ice crystals.
This omits invisible water vapour and ice crystals.
All three phases—gaseous, liquid, and solid—occur in the atmosphere.
This omits ice, which occurs in cold clouds and precipitation.

Cooling with unchanged moisture makes RH rise and the spread shrink.
The spread decreases, rather than increases, as temperature approaches dew point.
This is correct: cooling raises relative humidity and reduces the spread.
Cooling does not increase spread; RH rises while spread decreases.
Relative humidity rises toward 100%, not 0%, as cloud base is reached.
Cloud forms when the rising parcel cools to its own dew point.
An inversion may cap cloud growth but does not define the condensation level.
The parcel reaches its own dew point; environmental dew point is not the criterion.
Thunderstorm and shower are weather phenomena, not the two broad cloud forms.
The basic structural distinction is convective cumulus versus layered stratiform cloud.
Ice clouds are a phase/family subset, not the broad counterpart to stratiform clouds.
Clouds are classified by form as cumulus and stratiform, not simply lifted.
The bank-keyed image shows detached, vertically developed cumulus cloud.
Cirrus are high, wispy ice clouds, unlike the keyed cumulus form.
Stratus is a uniform layer, not the keyed detached convective cloud.
“Altus” is not a cloud type; alto- denotes middle-level cloud forms.
Stratus is a flat layer, not the bank-keyed high wispy cloud.
Cumulus has a cauliflower appearance, unlike the keyed cirrus.
Altocumulus forms middle-level patches or rolls, not high wisps.
The bank key identifies cirrus, the high, fibrous ice-cloud type.
Spread helps locate the cloud base, not usually the cumulus top.
Relative humidity influences moisture but an inversion is the typical cap on vertical growth.
An inversion suppresses vertical motion and can limit cumulus cloud tops.
Absolute humidity alone does not impose the vertical cap that an inversion creates.
A small temperature–dew-point spread and falling temperature bring air toward saturation.
Rising temperature generally enlarges the spread and reduces fog tendency.
Strong winds usually mix the air and are not the typical radiation-fog setup.
Low pressure is not the direct indicator; cooling toward dew point is.
Haze consists of aerosols and is less directly sensitive to temperature than water-droplet fog.
Radiation fog forms by cooling to dew point, so temperature strongly affects it.
Patches of fog are water droplets and respond to temperature and mixing.
Mist consists of suspended water droplets, which are temperature-sensitive.
A low spread favours saturation and fog; it does not prevent it.
Clear skies permit strong night-time radiative cooling and favour radiation fog.
Light or calm wind allows near-surface cooling and can favour radiation fog.
Overcast clouds reduce outgoing night-time radiation and can prevent radiation fog.
Calm wind and sunlight alone do not grow precipitation particles; cloud dynamics matter.
Humidity and warmth alone do not ensure particles grow large enough to fall.
Moderate or strong updrafts support droplet/ice-particle growth to precipitation size.
An inversion suppresses vertical growth, making precipitation development less favourable.
Strong updrafts keep particles aloft for growth and are required for larger precipitation particles.
An inversion caps vertical development rather than promoting precipitation growth.
Strong horizontal wind alone does not provide the necessary cloud updraft.
Cloud-base height is not the controlling requirement for particle growth.
Central Europe is not influenced only by Arctic and polar air; tropical air also arrives.
Tropical and Arctic omits the major polar maritime/continental influences.
Equatorial air rarely directly dominates Central European weather.
Central Europe is mainly affected by polar cold and tropical warm air masses.
Temperature at origin and present region alone does not describe source and route.
Environmental lapse rate is not the defining classification of an air mass.
Wind speed and tropopause height do not determine the air-mass identity.
Source region and subsequent track determine its properties and modification.
Continental tropical air is hot, not the winter Russian source described.
Maritime tropical air originates over warm oceans and is moist.
Maritime polar air is cool and moist, not continental from Russia.
A Russian winter source is continental polar: cP.
The lower troposphere warms over spring/summer land; upper-layer warming is not the cause.
Increasing relative humidity alone does not explain the destabilisation.
A warmer surface heats the lower polar air and steepens the lapse rate, destabilising it.
Warming from below destabilises polar air rather than stabilising it.
A front aloft is not the bank-keyed surface warm-front symbol.
The keyed symbol is a warm front, shown by semicircles on one side.
Cold fronts use triangles, not the bank-keyed warm-front semicircles.
Occlusion uses alternating triangles and semicircles on the same side.
Ci-to-Ns steady rain describes a typical warm-front sequence, not cold-front passage.
Calm dissipation or winter high fog is not the typical active cold-front band.
This describes a sea-breeze cycle, not a cold front.
Cold fronts bring a narrow band of Cb/showers, gusts, then Cu with isolated showers.
The bank-keyed symbol is a cold front, identified by triangles.
Occlusion shows both triangle and semicircle symbols on the same side.
A front aloft is not the keyed surface cold-front line.
Cold-front triangles point in the direction of movement.
Clear skies and good visibility are not expected within the active frontal band.
Near a cold front, heavy showers, turbulence, possible thunderstorms, and moderate visibility are typical.
Visibility below 1 km with continuous precipitation is more characteristic of severe fog/warm-front conditions.
Isolated high cloud alone misses the cold-front showers and turbulence.
This could describe pre-frontal or settled conditions; post-front weather includes showers and Cu.
Behind a cold front, visibility often improves with Cu and isolated rain or snow showers.
Lowering cloud and prolonged precipitation are more typical ahead of a warm front.
Poor visibility and widespread stratus are not the usual post-cold-front pattern.
A front aloft is not the bank-keyed occluded surface front.
A warm front has semicircles only on one side.
Occlusion has alternating triangles and semicircles on the same side of the line.
A cold front has triangles, not both symbol types together.
Seasonal northwest/southwest directions are not the usual polar-low track rule.
The low commonly moves parallel to the isobars in its warm sector.
The warm-front line is not the governing steering direction.
This seasonal directional claim is not the standard movement description.
The bank expects veering during passage of both fronts, not backing after the cold front.
The keyed rule is veering at passage of both warm and cold fronts.
Backing at both passages contradicts the bank’s expected veer.
The bank expects veering, not backing, during warm-front passage.
30-055.note: For this bank question, interpret “during passage” as veering at both fronts; wind may back ahead of a warm front.

why: Cold air aloft destabilises the column and favours showers and thunderstorms.
Calm weather and lifted fog are not typical of an unstable upper trough.
A trough/cold pool aloft does not favour stable, widespread stratus as its main outcome.
Shallow Cu and calm wind understate the convection favoured by a trough.
Cold air aloft increases instability and can trigger showers and thunderstorms.
Frontal weather requires a boundary between air masses; cold inflow aloft alone is not that.
Cold air aloft promotes instability rather than stabilisation.
It tends to build convection, not simply dissipate cloud.
Squall lines and thunderstorms are not typical of widespread summer high pressure.
Nimbostratus and prolonged rain are not usual beneath a summer anticyclone.
Overcast low stratus is more associated with winter moisture trapped beneath an inversion.
Summer high pressure commonly allows scattered fair-weather cumulus.
Widespread high fog is chiefly a winter anticyclone issue, not the summer pattern.
Summer high pressure brings subsidence, cloud dissipation, and perhaps a few high Cu.
Passing fronts describe unsettled weather rather than a settled high.
Squall lines and thunderstorms are not typical of broad summer high pressure.
Widely spaced isobars mean weak gradient; local winds can dominate.
Small spacing means a strong gradient, inconsistent with calm local-wind conditions.
Tight isobars indicate strong winds, not a calm summer anticyclone.
Widely spaced isobars do not support strong prevailing westerlies.
Large isobar spacing means weak, not strong, prevailing wind.
A weak pressure gradient allows variable winds and local breezes to dominate.
Strong westerlies need a tighter gradient, not widely spaced isobars.
Local systems may form, but strong prevailing westerlies contradict the weak gradient.
Foehn develops when stable air is driven across a mountain ridge.
Calm high pressure does not force air over a ridge to create foehn.
Stability is relevant, but foehn also requires cross-ridge flow, not calm conditions.
Unstable air may produce convection; classic foehn involves stable cross-mountain flow.
Smooth Ns with steady precipitation fits stable layered ascent, not humid unstable convection.
Unstable moist air forced upslope can build embedded Cb, showers, hail, and thunderstorms.
Thin high cloud and light steady precipitation describe a layered warm-front process.
Low stratus without precipitation does not fit forced ascent of unstable humid air.
The keyed lee-side wave cloud is lenticularis, lens-shaped at a standing-wave crest.
Castellanus has turreted cloud tops and signals instability, not the wave-lens form.
Nimbostratus is a widespread precipitation layer, not a lee wave marker.
Cumulonimbus is a convective tower, unlike the keyed lenticular wave cloud.

Very cold ice-crystal cloud alone lacks the supercooled liquid water needed for usual airframe accretion.
Clear air has no visible supercooled liquid water for airframe ice accretion.
The range includes above-freezing air and hail is not the required supercooled droplet condition.
At −20 to −40°C, supercooled liquid water is generally less prevalent than in the critical range.
The range includes above-freezing temperatures, which do not support airframe icing.
The most dangerous exam range is 0 to −12°C with supercooled droplets.
The range extends to +5°C; the key icing danger is near freezing in sub-zero air.
Stratiform cloud does not guarantee turbulence below it.
Thermal convection beneath cumulus causes turbulence below the cloud.

An inversion can suppress vertical motion; it is not where turbulence must always occur.
Cu coverage alone does not make severe wind shear especially likely.
A nearby shower can produce downdrafts and a gust front, creating severe low-level shear.
Thirty minutes after a shower is not the specific high-risk situation given by the key.
Ci ahead of a warm front does not imply severe shear by itself.
Warm dry air plus a strong inversion suppresses convection and storm growth.
Thunderstorms favour warm humid air and conditional instability, with a lifting trigger.
Cold stable air under stratus is not the typical thunderstorm environment.
A clear cold night with fog lacks the warm, moist unstable conditions.
Thermal storms need instability plus warm, moist air; low temperature and humidity oppose them.
Absolute stability suppresses the vertical motion needed for a thermal storm.
High humidity helps, but absolute stability prevents convective storm development.
Thermal thunderstorms favour conditionally unstable air with warm, humid low levels.
Mature storms contain strong updrafts and downdrafts, with heavy precipitation and hazards.
The developing cumulus stage is dominated by updrafts, not both strong motions.
“Thunderstorm stage” is not the three-stage classification used here.
Downdrafts dominate the dissipating stage as updrafts weaken.
The mature stage has both updrafts and downdrafts.
The developing cumulus stage is dominated by strong updrafts.
“Upwind stage” is not a standard thunderstorm life-cycle stage.
Downdrafts dominate dissipation, not the growing stage.
Cabin depressurisation is not the main direct lightning hazard.
Lightning can overheat and damage the aircraft skin and exposed components.
Cockpit equipment does not ordinarily explode; electrical interference is a secondary effect.
Radio static may occur, but surface/exposed-part damage is the principal keyed danger.
Heavy shower and thunderstorm precipitation downdrafts cause strong low-level shear.
Radiation fog on a cold clear night does not produce convective downdrafts.
A sea breeze can cause a boundary but is not the specific heavy-downdraft hazard.
High flattened Cu without heavy showers is less likely to produce severe downdrafts.

Calm high stratus is not the typical windward forced-lift effect.
Dissipation and gusty warming describe the lee-side descent, not windward weather.
Scattered Cu with storms is not the classic stable foehn windward pattern.

The windward side does not become the main rotor hazard merely because cloud is thick.
Low stratus does not indicate the severe lee-wave rotor turbulence described.
Unbroken cloud overhead alone does not indicate mountain-wave rotor turbulence.

Satellite imagery shows broad cloud cover and frontal structure.
